entities.name: Cabinet of Turkey
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Cabinet of Turkey (Bakanlar Kurulu), substantially transformed by the 2017 constitutional referendum and 2018 elections from a parliamentary cabinet model to an executive presidential system, represents one of the most significant constitutional transitions in a NATO member state's modern history — concentrating executive power in the presidency under Recep Tayyip Erdoğan while eliminating the Prime Minister role and dramatically reshaping Turkey's governance structure.

Turkey's cabinet operated under a parliamentary model from the republic's founding by Atatürk in 1923 through 2018: the Prime Minister (from the majority parliamentary coalition) led the cabinet, while the President was a largely ceremonial figure. Under this system, Turkey experienced multiple military coups (1960, 1971, 1980, 1997 'postmodern coup') as the military treated itself as guardian of secularism. The AKP's rise (2002) and Erdoğan's consolidation of power gradually challenged this structure.

The April 2017 constitutional referendum — passed 51.4% to 48.6% amid disputed fairness — replaced parliamentary government with an executive presidential system, abolishing the Prime Ministership (held by Ahmet Davutoğlu, then Binali Yıldırım). Since June 2018, Turkey's cabinet ministers are directly appointed by and accountable solely to the President, without parliamentary confirmation. This transition has been criticized by opposition parties and democratic governance observers as concentrating power incompatible with democratic checks and balances, while defenders argue it ended the political instability of coalition governments.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Turkey's cabinet system — transformed by the 2017 executive presidential transition from parliamentary to personal-presidential governance, concentrating power in Erdoğan, and representing a major democratic backslide in a NATO member — is one of the most consequential constitutional transitions in post-Cold War European politics.
